items.title: Buddy Collette interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, February 13, 1999
items.q: well even when we had the Chico band before I had my group, the Chico quintet, we played in Long Beach

ctx.x: No it wasn’t segregated, it was always integrated. Because, well even when we had the Chico band before I had my group, the Chico quintet, we played in Long Beach, and there weren’t as many blacks there as there are say now. At that time there were very few other than whites coming in the club but that was just because not too many people lived there then and then later on the people would come from L.A. because Sleepy Stein, who was a disc jockey and still is I guess, and the owner there, Harry Rubin, put radio…
It really did have a very unique sound, especially with the bop that was going on at the time, to all of a sudden have this different instrumentation.

items.title: Chico Hamilton interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 30, 2000
items.q: The group was intact with Buddy and Jim Hall, and Carson. And Buddy and I came up musically together.

ctx.x: That sound with the cello and pianoless. Did that come about from sitting down and thinking let’s find something different here? Or was it a more practical—

Originally the group was going to be French horn, John Graas, he was the number one French horn player on the West Coast at that time when I formed the group. The group was intact with Buddy and Jim Hall, and Carson. And Buddy and I came up musically together. Cars and I were with Gerry together, and Jim Hall was just a stroke of luck. He needed a gig and he heard that I was organizing, putting a group together. Because he was stacking music in a music store at that time. He wasn’t even playing. And the day of…
And even had the part where the stick fell.

items.title: Chico Hamilton — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I called rehearsal. I already had Buddy. You know, talked with Buddy.

ctx.x: Let’s talk about why is it that you’re forming a group at this point that has this particular combination of instruments. I think that that’s something that historians would love for you to be able to express.

In all honesty that happened just by sheer accident. How I come about with the original quintet is that at first I wanted to get Gerry Wiggins, get a piano trio, but all the piano players that I liked, man, they had their own thing going so I decided to try something else. So I don’t know how I got in contact with Jim Hall.
